title: Divide Ladder
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of this chapter. An adult sees a child dividing over and over. What is actually being settled is why the run has to be unbroken: a number never tried is a number that cannot be ruled out, and a list built by trying whichever divisors came to mind is a collection rather than a list. The printed run that this topic is built from promises serial order and then leaves one number out, which is exactly the move the ladder refuses.

writeup.why: Find every factor of a number by dividing by each whole number in turn, and find out why the run must not skip one.
writeup.look: A ladder of rungs up the middle with a tray of countable things above it, a shelf for whatever will not fit, and a fenced pen of factor cards beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Divide Ladder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the rungs tried against the rungs the ladder is built for, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each trial settles and the second fixed at the height of the ladder, with the number of cards standing in the pen beside them. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The ladder stands up the middle of the working area, 180 wide by 528 at 508,202, its rungs 56 tall and numbered from one at the foot upward, with the number tray above it at 508,202 holding the chosen number drawn as that many identical countable things, never more than twenty under one visible tie. Stepping on a rung opens the sharing board to the right of the ladder, 462 by 400 at 700,202: the tray empties onto it as that many rows, drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable, each row shut off from the next by a drawn wall rather than by a change of colour. Where the sharing does not come out, whatever will not fit travels to the leftover shelf, 462 by 92 at 700,618, which sits OUTSIDE the rows on the same surface at full strength and fully countable, is never faded, never crossed out and never tucked under a row, and holds what it was given for the rest of the run. A rung tapped while a lower rung is still untried does not open: the untried rung lights, is named, and nothing else is given away, so the refusal teaches the order rather than the answer. Every rung that comes out sends two cards into the factor pen, 424 by 400 at 64,202, one carrying the number stepped on and one carrying the number in each row; the pen has a wall at its left end and a wall at its right and the cards lie in order between them, so the list is drawn closed while it is still being built. The repeat light sits above the pen at 64,142, dark until a card lands on one already inside, and the ladder stops climbing the instant it comes on. The tick and cross bay runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 76 at 64,654: a smaller number and a bigger one are dropped into it, one division runs on the board, and a tick or a cross is drawn with the remainder standing beside it. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a quotient, a remainder or a count of factors is asked for, and on the first phase a word pad of the ladder's own words, factor, divides, exactly, leftover, remainder and nothing over, so that a trial can be judged with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a trial that failed is told by the leftover standing outside its rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it before it is told by anything else. A rung that failed is never dimmed and never cleared as the ladder climbs past it. Its rows and its leftover stay drawn where they were, because a run with its failures rubbed out looks exactly like a run that never made them, and that likeness is the whole trouble with the page this tool is built from.
writeup.finish: The card shows the tallest ladder the child climbed, every failed rung with its leftover still showing, and the full pen beside it.

phases.win: one rung lights with level rows and the other leaves its remainder standing outside them
phases.does: steps on each rung in turn and looks at what is left on the shelf
phases.goal: a factor divides the number and leaves nothing over
phases.says: Share them out. Which try left nothing over? That one is a factor.
phases.check: Away from the screen: share 20 counters onto 4 plates, then onto 6. Which of those two numbers is a factor of 20, and how did the counters tell you?
phases.feels: a trial that leaves something over has answered, and the thing it left is the answer
phases.hands: Put twenty counters on the table and share them onto four plates, one at a time, going round. Then sweep them up and share the same twenty onto six plates the same way. Both times, before anybody says an answer, put whatever will not go round again in the middle of the table where everyone can see it and count it out loud. Ask which of the two numbers is a factor of twenty, and what the pile in the middle has to say about the other one.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many things are standing outside the rows? Second rung, the phase's: what does anything standing outside the rows say about this trial? Third rung: the tray is cut to twelve things and the child steps on three and then on five and looks at both shelves. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: two left out of twenty looks like a rounding off rather than a failure, and once they are out of sight the six rows sitting there look every bit as finished as the four rows did.
wrong.move: calls six a factor of twenty because it very nearly went in, and brushes the two that would not fit off the side of the tray.
wrong.screen: the sharing runs again at walking pace and the two are carried to the leftover shelf outside the rows, at full strength and countable, where they stay. The six rows are then counted out one at a time, three in each, and the board is read as eighteen; the tray it came from is read as twenty. The child's verdict stays in the answer slot the whole time and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: sharing has meant everybody getting some for as long as they have been sharing anything, and two things left over read as a problem to be tidied away rather than as the answer to the question.
wrong.move: shares the two left over out as well, splitting them between the rows so that every row comes out the same.
wrong.screen: the two are drawn whole and set on the shelf, and the rows are rebuilt from the tray with only whole things in them. The tool asks how many whole things went into each row and the board answers three, with the two still standing outside; the four plate sharing is then laid beside it with its shelf empty, and the two boards are left standing together.

phases.screen: a full tray with two rungs offered, one that comes out and one that does not
phases.soWhat: A factor divides the number and leaves nothing over, and anything standing outside the rows says it is not one.
phases.concept: What makes a number a factor

phases.win: every rung carries either level rows or a leftover, and no rung is blank
phases.does: climbs one rung at a time and tries to jump one, which is refused
phases.goal: the run is unbroken, and a trial that fails is still written down
phases.says: Start at the bottom and take every rung. Try to jump one and see what happens.
phases.check: The book's own run goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9. Which number never got a line, and what does 18 shared into that many rows leave?
phases.feels: a run with a hole in it looks exactly like a run without one
phases.hands: Write the factor pair run for eighteen out on squared paper exactly as the page prints it: one times eighteen, two times nine, three times six, then four fails, then six, seven, eight and nine. Read the run aloud and ask which whole number never got a line. Work that missing line together, eighteen shared into five rows, and write it in where it belongs. Then find the factors of forty the same way, with a line for every whole number from one to ten and not one of them left out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which is the lowest rung with nothing written on it yet? Second rung, the phase's: can a number you never tried be ruled out? Third rung: the ladder is cut to six rungs with a small number in the tray and the child climbs it from the foot with no rung skipped. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: nothing in a written list says which numbers were tried, so a run with a hole in it comes out looking exactly like a run without one, and the child who skipped is never contradicted by the page.
wrong.move: jumps from two straight to four, because three has an odd look to it and the run is long.
wrong.screen: the ladder refuses to open the fourth rung and lights the third, naming it and giving nothing else away. When the third rung is taken it comes out at once, six rows of three with the shelf empty, and two cards drop into the pen. The pen is then read out with those two cards lifted and standing to one side, so that the list the skip would have produced and the list the run produced are up together.

wrong.why: a list of factors is what was asked for, so a row that produced no factor looks like a row not worth the ink, and the shorter page looks tidier.
wrong.move: keeps only the rungs that came out and leaves the failed trials off the paper altogether.
wrong.screen: two ladders are drawn side by side, one carrying every rung from one upward and one carrying only the rungs that lit. Both are read out and both give the same six numbers. A rung is then quietly taken out of the second ladder and it is read again: nothing on it has changed and nothing anywhere says a trial is missing. The first ladder keeps its blank rung lit.

phases.screen: the ladder from the foot upward with every rung blank and waiting
phases.soWhat: Work up from one and try every whole number in turn, and write down the trials that fail as well as the ones that come out.
phases.concept: Working up through the numbers in order

phases.win: two cards land in the pen from one rung and the pen count goes up by two
phases.does: reads the number stepped on and the number in each row, and drops both into the pen
phases.goal: one exact division puts two numbers into the list
phases.says: You made one division. How many factors has it just given you?
phases.check: 51 divided by 3 is 17. Which two factors of 51 has that one division handed you?
phases.feels: one sharing, and two cards land in the pen together
phases.hands: Lay twenty-seven counters out in three equal rows and ask for both numbers on the board to be said aloud, three rows and nine in each. Write both into the factor list. Then turn the board a quarter turn, so the same counters read as nine rows of three, and ask whether that is a new fact or the one already written. Do it again with fifty-six counters in seven rows and see how many entries one sharing is worth.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many rows are on the board? Second rung, the phase's: how many are in each row, and is that a factor too? Third rung: the tray is cut to twelve things, the child steps on two, and both cards are dropped in by hand. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the rung is the thing the finger touched and the thing the question seemed to be about, while the number in each row arrives as the result of the work rather than as another answer.
wrong.move: writes down the number stepped on and lets the number in each row go, so the pen fills one card at a time.
wrong.screen: the board is turned a quarter turn in front of the child, the same twenty-seven counters reading as nine rows of three, and the ladder steps itself onto the ninth rung to show that rung coming out on the same tray. The card the child did put in the pen stays exactly where it was put, and the one that was let go is drawn lying on the board beside its row with the pen wall open beside it.

wrong.why: every rung produces a number stepped on and a number in each row whether it comes out or not, and the leftover sits off at the side of the board where it is easy to stop counting it.
wrong.move: drops two cards in for a rung where something was left over, because a division was still done and two numbers still came out of it.
wrong.screen: the leftover lights on its shelf and is counted out. The rows are counted beside it, four rows of six, and the board is read as twenty-four against a tray of twenty-seven. The two cards spring back out of the pen with nothing marked, the pen count drops back to what it was, and the rung is left standing as a failure with its three still outside the rows.

phases.screen: a rung that has just come out, with the empty pen beside it
phases.soWhat: Every division that comes out exactly gives you the number you divided by and the answer, and both of them are factors.
phases.concept: Every exact division hands you two

phases.win: the repeat light comes on, the ladder stops and the pen is read out as finished
phases.does: carries on climbing until a card lands on one already in the pen
phases.goal: the list is finished when the answers repeat what is already there
phases.says: Keep going. Tell me the moment an answer is one you have already written.
phases.check: You are finding the factors of 96, and 5 and 7 have both just failed. May you stop there? Say what you would lose.
phases.feels: the moment an answer is one you have already written, there is nothing new left to find
phases.hands: Climb forty-five on squared paper, a line for every whole number from one upward, and write both numbers of every division that comes out. Stop the moment somebody notices an answer they have already written and ring it. Then start on ninety-six and stop deliberately early, straight after six, because five and seven have both just failed. Write out the list as it stands, then carry the run on to the repeat and see which two numbers the early stop had lost.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which answer has just come out of the division? Second rung, the phase's: is that number already standing in the pen? Third rung: the ladder is cut to a small number and the child climbs it to the repeat and reads the pen out. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: a run of trials that give nothing feels like the end of the number, and the list standing in the pen is long enough by then to look like an answer rather than like part of one.
wrong.move: stops after a couple of failures in a row and calls the list complete, because the pen already looks respectably full.
wrong.screen: the ladder carries on from where the child stopped, one rung at a time, with every rung that was never climbed lit in order as it is reached. The pen the child left is kept drawn exactly as it stood, beside the pen the finished run builds, and the two are read against each other card by card so that the cards the early stop never had are the only ones standing alone. Nothing is marked.

wrong.why: the ladder still has rungs on it and stopping while there is anything left to try feels like leaving the job half done, and a longer list looks like a better one.
wrong.move: keeps climbing past the repeat all the way to the number itself, writing every pair down a second time.
wrong.screen: the repeat light stays on and the ladder is allowed to climb. Every rung above the repeat does come out, and every card it sends lands on one already lying in the pen and is drawn settling on top of it rather than beside it. The pen count in the corner is held in view throughout and never moves, and the whole of the child's extra work stays drawn on the ladder.

phases.screen: the ladder well up with the pen already holding most of the list
phases.soWhat: Stop when the answers begin to repeat what is already in the pen, and not when the failures have made you tired.

writeup.delight: The third phase, at the instant a rung comes out. The rows settle level on the board and the two cards leave together, one lifting off the rung the child stepped on and one lifting off the end of a row, and they travel side by side along a drawn path into the pen and land as a linked pair. Drag either card back out and the other follows it, because the two came from one division and neither of them was found on its own. The count in the corner goes up by two on the way in and down by two on the way back, the rows on the board never move, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a full tray stands at the top of the ladder with exactly two rungs offered under it, one that will come out and one that will not, and the leftover shelf empty and ruled. On the second the ladder stands from the foot upward with every rung blank and the tray already loaded. On the third a single rung has just come out, its rows lying level on the board, with the factor pen beside it empty and its two end walls up. On the fourth the ladder is well climbed, most of the pen is full, and the repeat light above it is dark. The running count at the top left holds the rungs tried against the rungs the ladder is built for, with the count of cards in the pen beside them, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the lower of the two offered rungs, or the rung at the foot, or the pair of numbers lying on the settled rows, or the next untried rung, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what sharing the tray out that way would leave behind. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any number up to a hundred in the tray, with the pen, the leftover shelf and the repeat light switched on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on testing a single divisor, working the run in order without skipping, reading two factors out of one division, and saying when the list is finished.
voiceLines: A tray of things up at the top, and a ladder of trials under it.
Share them out. Which try left nothing over? That one is a factor.
Start at the bottom and take every rung. Try to jump one and see what happens.
You made one division. How many factors has it just given you?
Keep going. Tell me the moment an answer is one you have already written.
Another number in the tray. Start at the foot and take every rung.
Free play. Any number in the tray, with the pen, the shelf and the repeat light as you like.
Share them out again, slowly. What is standing outside the rows?
Every rung tried in order, every failure still showing, and the pen full.

observations.why: A trial that fails rules a number out, and a number that was never ruled out is a number never tried.
observations.soWhat: The failures are part of the working, and a list with them rubbed out cannot be checked.
observations.observe: The trials that failed stayed on the ladder with their leftovers standing beside them.

observations.why: A number that is skipped can still be a factor, and nothing later in the run says it was missed.
observations.soWhat: The run starts at one and takes every whole number in turn.
observations.observe: The ladder would not open a rung while a lower one was still blank.

observations.why: The number divided by and the answer both divide the number exactly, so both are factors of it.
observations.soWhat: The list grows two at a time, and writing down only the divisor writes down half of it.
observations.observe: One exact division put two cards in the pen, never one.

observations.why: Past that point every pair is one already found with its two numbers swapped over.
observations.soWhat: The repeat is the stop signal, and running out of patience is not.
observations.observe: The pen stopped filling at the moment a card landed on one already inside.

description: Climb a number one trial at a time, keep every rung that fails, and watch each exact division hand you two factors.

source_tool.name: Divide Ladder
source_tool.blurb: Climb a number one trial at a time, keep every rung that fails, and watch each exact division hand you two factors.

serves.exercise: dividing twelve into equal parts with colours, with three of the four star grids left blank
finding the factors of the six given numbers by division
ticking or crossing the ten printed pairs according to whether the smaller number is a factor of the bigger

source_tool.description: A ladder stands up the middle of the stage with one rung for each whole number, starting at one at the foot and climbing. The number being taken apart sits in a tray at the top as that many countable things. Stepping onto a rung shares the tray out into that many equal rows: where it comes out, the rows are drawn level and the rung lights, and where it does not, whatever will not fit is set down OUTSIDE the rows at full strength and stays there, so a trial that failed is a thing on the stage rather than a gap. A rung cannot be jumped. Reaching past one names the rung that has not been tried and will not go further until it has, which is the whole reason for working in order. Every rung that lights drops TWO cards into a factor pen beside the ladder, the number stepped on and the number in each row, so the list is seen to grow two at a time. A repeat light comes on the moment a card lands on one already in the pen, and that is the signal that there is nothing left to find. A tick and cross bay at the side takes a smaller number and a bigger one and runs the single trial that settles them.
source_tool.art_direction: A ladder of trials, a factor pen / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: trays of countable things, ruled rows on a board, a ladder of rungs with one trial to a rung, a pen with a wall at each end, a track of equal steps, cards that turn over, and two rings of cord that overlap.

Equal groups are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a row is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are in it, and the rows are kept apart by a drawn wall or a plain gap and never by colour alone.

Whatever is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the rows, on the same surface, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never crossed out, never tucked under a row and never left to be guessed from a gap. The leftover is the reason a trial failed, so it is the last thing any stage may hide.

A list of factors is drawn penned in between one and the number itself, with both ends of the run plainly stopped by a wall or a final post, so the list can be seen to end. A list of multiples is drawn running from the number away to the right, and the track carrying it leaves the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, so the list can be seen not to end. The two never run the same way on one stage.

A run of trials is drawn unbroken. Every whole number from one up to the last one tried keeps its own rung or row, in order, with none left out, and a trial that fails is drawn and marked as a failure rather than dropped.
Where the digits of a number are added, every digit sits in its own cell, zeros included, and a cell holding a zero is drawn and counted in rather than left out of the line.
Nothing the child is asked to count one at a time comes to more than twenty things in one group. A larger quantity is a ruled array of identical tiles or a written numeral, never a loose heap.
A list is told apart by the wall or the open edge at its end first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a counter or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number that is built by multiplying is green, and anything standing in both lists at once is rose, and those three hold in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Whatever is left over, and any trial that fails, is vermilion; the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber; and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. All of that holds in greyscale, because a failed trial is told apart by the leftover drawn outside its row before it is told apart by colour, and a factor list is told apart from a list of multiples by the wall at each end of it before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Share them out again, slowly. What is standing outside the rows?
voice.onNext: Another number in the tray. Start at the foot and take every rung.
voice.opening: A tray of things up at the top, and a ladder of trials under it.
voice.onFinish: Every rung tried in order, every failure still showing, and the pen full.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any number in the tray, with the pen, the shelf and the repeat light as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: What makes a number a factor
Working up through the numbers in order
Every exact division hands you two

placement.where: Straight after one number has been shared out by hand into plates or dishes and the leftovers have been looked at. The tool is what stops a trial being skipped and keeps the failed trial on the stage, which a child writing a list can only do by choosing to.

answer_key.rule: A factor of a number divides it and leaves nothing over. To find every factor, divide by one, then by two, then by three, and keep going up through the whole numbers without skipping any. A division that does not come out exactly means that number is not a factor, and the row is still written down. Every division that does come out gives two factors, the number divided by and the answer. Stop when the answers are numbers already on the list, because nothing new can come after that.
answer_key.wrong: The rung opens again and the sharing is redone slowly, row by row, with whatever will not fit set down outside the rows and counted aloud. A rung that was jumped is lit and tried first. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 20 divided by 4 is 5 with nothing left over, so 4 is a factor of 20.
20 divided by 6 is 3 with 2 left over, and those 2 stay outside the rows.
Anything left over means 6 is not a factor, and there is no second test to try.
items.answer: 4 is a factor of 20 and 6 is not
items.question: Divide 20 by 4, then divide 20 by 6. Which of the two is a factor of 20?
items.checkpoint: A factor leaves nothing over, and leaving nothing over is the whole test.
items.misconception: Calling 6 a factor because it nearly goes in, and ignoring the 2 still standing outside.

steps: Divide by 1, then 2, then 3, then 4, and keep going up without leaving any out.
40 divided by 3 leaves 1 over, so 3 is not a factor, and that row is still written down.
The divisions that come out give 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20 and 40, which is eight factors.
items.answer: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 20 and 40, and the first trial that fails is 3
items.question: Find every factor of 40 by dividing by each whole number from 1 upwards, and name the first trial that fails.
items.checkpoint: Working up in order without skipping is what makes the list complete.
items.misconception: Jumping from 2 to 4 because 3 looks unlikely, which leaves a gap the list cannot account for.

steps: 3 divides 27 exactly, so 3 is a factor of 27.
The answer, 9, divides 27 exactly as well, because 9 threes make 27.
So one division puts two cards in the pen, and the list grows two at a time.
items.question: 27 divided by 3 is 9. How many factors of 27 has that one division handed you?
items.checkpoint: Every exact division gives the number you divided by and the answer, and both are factors.
items.misconception: Writing down only the number you divided by, and losing the answer it gave.

steps: 1 gives 45, 3 gives 15 and 5 gives 9, while 2 and 4 each leave something over.
At 9 the answer is 5, and 5 is already written down from an earlier rung.
Nothing new can come after that, so the list of six factors is finished.
items.answer: At 9, because its answer 5 is already in the pen, and the factors are 1, 3, 5, 9, 15 and 45
items.question: Climb the ladder for 45 and say at which rung the answers begin to repeat.
items.checkpoint: Stop when the answers coming out are numbers you have already written down.
items.misconception: Carrying on to the number itself, writing every pair twice and calling it a longer list.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Is 8 a factor of 68?
items.final_answer: No, because 68 divided by 8 is 8 with 4 left over

items.question: Is 6 a factor of 78?
items.final_answer: Yes, because 78 divided by 6 is 13 with nothing over

items.question: 51 divided by 3 is 17. Name the two factors of 51 that this one division gives.
Find every factor of 92 by dividing in turn.
A child finding the factors of 70 divides by 1, then 2, then jumps straight to 5. Which trials were skipped, and what would they have shown?
items.final_answer: 3 and 4 were skipped. 70 divided by 3 leaves 1 over and 70 divided by 4 leaves 2 over, so neither is a factor

items.question: 62 divided by 2 is 31. Which two factors does that give, and how many factors has 62 altogether?
items.final_answer: 2 and 31, and 62 has four factors: 1, 2, 31 and 62

items.question: Find every factor of 76 by dividing in turn, and say at which trial the answers begin to repeat.
items.final_answer: 1, 2, 4, 19, 38 and 76, and they begin to repeat at 19, whose answer 4 is already on the list

items.question: A child says 100 has an odd number of factors. Find them all and say whether that is right.
items.final_answer: Yes. 100 has nine factors, 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50 and 100, and the run stops at 10 because 10 tens make 100

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the number being taken apart as that many countable things
shares the tray into that many equal rows and lights the rung if it comes out
sets whatever will not fit outside the rows, countable and at full strength
names the rung that has not been tried and will not climb past it
takes the two cards each exact division gives, the divisor and the answer
comes on when a card lands on one already in the pen
runs the single trial that settles one pair of numbers

teaching_notes: Share a real number of counters out onto plates by hand before the tool is opened, and make the leftovers the thing everybody looks at. Then use the tool for what paper will not do: stop at a trial that fails and refuse to move on until somebody has said, out loud, why the row still gets written. That is the whole idea of the topic, and the chapter's own worked run is missing it, so a class reading the page will not meet it unless it is staged. Keep the no skipping control locked for the first few numbers and let a child try to jump a rung on purpose. When a rung lights, ask how many factors it just gave before anybody touches the pen: the answer is two, every single time, and a child who says one is writing half the list. The tick and cross bay is worth a few minutes of its own, because judging one pair is a single division and children slow it down by listing factors they were never asked for. Finish by asking how they know the list is complete. Because the answers started repeating is the right answer; because it looks long enough is not.
generation_prompt: Build a trial division tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A vertical ladder of rungs runs up the middle, numbered from one at the foot upward, with a tray at the top holding the chosen number drawn as that many identical countable things, never more than twenty to a visible group. Tapping a rung shares the tray into that many equal rows on a ruled board, drawing exactly that many rows with exactly the same number in each, separated by drawn walls rather than by colour. Where the sharing does not come out, whatever is left is animated onto a shelf OUTSIDE the rows at full strength, fully countable, never faded and never tucked under a row, and it stays there for the rest of the run. A rung tapped while an earlier rung is untried is refused: the untried rung lights and is named, and nothing else is given away. Every rung that comes out sends two cards into a fenced factor pen beside the ladder, one carrying the number stepped on and one carrying the number in each row, and the pen has a wall at each end so the list is visibly closed rather than open. A repeat light above the pen comes on the instant a card matches one already in it, and the ladder stops climbing. A side bay takes a smaller and a bigger number, runs the single division that settles whether the smaller is a factor of the bigger, and draws a tick or a cross with the remainder beside it. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put a number in the tray. Step on every rung from the bottom up. Do not skip one. If something is left over, leave it on the shelf where you can see it. Each rung that comes out gives you two factors, so put both in the pen. Stop when an answer is one you already have.
